prompt.context: Our client is a used car dealership whose business has been stagnating in recent years. They are located in a low to middle-income area and in the past have only sold cars to customers who are willing to pay 100% of the cost up-front or can achieve bank financing. In order to boost sales, our client is considering offering loans to customers that the dealership itself will finance. To be eligible for a loan, customers must undergo a complete credit check (which we assume to be accurate). The credit check rates potential car buyers on a scale of 0 to 100, where 0 corresponds to a 0% chance of paying off the loan and 100 corresponds to a 100% chance of paying the loan in full. Each loan lasts 1 year in which payments are made monthly and the entire loan will be paid off in 1 year's time. Buyers ultimately fall into two categories: those that pay off the loan entirely, and those that default.
prompt.question: What should be the cutoff credit score level at which we decide to give potential buyers a loan? What issues might cause you to alter this cutoff level?

clarifying_info.q: What is the average cost of a car to the dealership?
What is the average price the car is sold to the customer?
Is there a minimum down payment requirement?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the minimum down payment is $1,000 regardless of credit rating.

clarifying_info.q: When do defaulters typically stop paying?
clarifying_info.a: The average loan defaulter makes three months of payments before defaulting.

clarifying_info.q: Does the dealership make money on the loans themselves (interest)?
clarifying_info.a: Assume we make nothing on the loans; they are only used to entice in additional customers.

clarifying_info.q: Does the default amount correspond proportionally to the credit rating?
clarifying_info.a: No. All defaulters default after an average of three months regardless of their credit rating.

framework: Cost-Revenue and Profitability analysis: determine the profit per successful loan vs. the loss per default
Calculate the breakeven ratio of good loans to bad loans needed
Translate that breakeven ratio into a minimum credit score cutoff
Discuss qualitative factors and risk considerations that might push the cutoff higher or lower

questions.prompt: What is the profit per car sold to a customer who pays in full (either upfront or via a fully repaid loan)?
questions.guidance: The dealership buys at $6,000 and sells at $7,000, so gross profit per car is $1,000.

math.setup: Selling price minus cost to dealership
math.answer: $1,000 profit per car sold and fully paid

questions.prompt: How much does the dealership lose on a defaulted loan?
questions.guidance: A defaulter pays a $1,000 down payment and then makes 3 monthly payments. The remaining loan amount is $6,000 (selling price minus down payment). Monthly payment = $6,000 / 12 = $500. Three payments = $1,500. Total received from defaulter = $1,000 + $1,500 = $2,500. Cost of car = $6,000. Net loss = $6,000 - $2,500 = $3,500.

math.setup: Cost of car minus total cash received from defaulter
steps: Loss = cost of car - total received = $6,000 - $2,500 = $3,500

questions.prompt: How many successful (fully repaid) loans are needed to offset one default? What does this imply for the minimum credit score cutoff?
questions.guidance: Each good loan earns $1,000 profit; each bad loan loses $3,500. To break even, need 3.5 good loans per 1 bad loan, i.e., 4 good loans for every 1 bad loan (rounding up). This means at least 4 out of 5 loans (80%) must be good. Since the credit score equals the probability of full repayment, the breakeven cutoff is a credit score of 80.

math.setup: Number of good loans needed to offset one default
steps: Break-even ratio: $3,500 / $1,000 = 3.5 good loans per 1 default
Round up: 4 good loans needed for every 1 default
Credit score = probability of repayment, so minimum score = 80

questions.prompt: What factors might cause you to adjust the cutoff above or below 80?
questions.guidance: Strong answer covers: (1) raising the cutoff to start conservatively given operational uncertainty; (2) cash flow / solvency risk — a few consecutive defaults could bankrupt a small dealership; (3) economic outlook — expect cutoff to rise in a downturn; (4) ability to change the risk profile by raising the minimum down payment, allowing a lower cutoff; (5) add-ons or warranties paid upfront reduce risk exposure; (6) at exactly 80 the dealer works hard for slim margins, so 90+ offers much better risk-reward.

brainstorming.prompt: What alternative levers or structural changes could the dealership use to manage default risk and potentially lower the credit score cutoff?

categories.name: Down payment adjustments
ideas: Require higher minimum down payments for lower credit scores to change the risk profile
Offer tiered down payments: lower score = higher required down payment

categories.name: Add-ons and prepaid products
ideas: Sell warranties or service contracts paid upfront to increase cash received before default risk materializes
Bundle insurance products paid at purchase

categories.name: Operational conservatism
ideas: Start with a higher cutoff (e.g., 90) and lower it gradually as experience and cash reserves grow
Cap total number of financed loans at any given time to limit exposure

categories.name: Economic and external monitoring
ideas: Raise the cutoff during economic downturns when default probability increases
Monitor local employment trends in the low-to-middle income area

categories.name: Loan structure changes
ideas: Shorten loan term to reduce exposure window
Require larger monthly payments early in the loan

categories.name: Portfolio diversification
ideas: Spread financed loans across many customers to reduce concentration risk
Establish a reserve fund from profits on good loans to absorb defaults

recommendation: Set the minimum credit score cutoff at 80, as this is the mathematical breakeven point where the profit from fully repaid loans offsets losses from defaults (4 good loans needed per 1 bad loan)
In practice, recommend starting at a cutoff of 90 to build operational experience and reserves before expanding to riskier borrowers
risks: A string of consecutive defaults could create cash flow problems or insolvency for a small dealership
Economic deterioration in the low-to-middle income area could cause actual default rates to exceed credit score predictions
The credit check is assumed accurate — any inaccuracy would shift the real breakeven cutoff
next_steps: Assess the dealership's current cash reserves to determine how many consecutive defaults they could absorb
Monitor portfolio performance quarterly and adjust the cutoff as data accumulates
Explore raising minimum down payments or selling prepaid warranties to improve the risk profile and potentially serve lower credit-score customers profitably
